info.disambiguation: Canadian record producer, guitarist, vocalist, and songwriter
info.bio:
Daniel Lanois es productor y músico. Nació el 19 de Septiembre de 1951 en Hull, Quebec, Canadá  aunque es de nacionalidad franco-canadiense. Calificado como ''el productor más importante emergido en los Ochenta'' por la Rolling Stone; ha producido discos de muchos artistas destacados como u2, Peter Gabriel, Bob Dylan, y Brian Eno. También ha compuesto álbumes propios. 
Producciones:

Achtung Baby 1991 - U2
The Joshua Tree 1987 - U2
All That You Can't Leave Behind 2000- U2

scenes.name: Cantautores de los ochenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Absorbida la new wave, el mundo de los cantautores no vuelve a ser el mismo: los referentes pasan a ser Dylan, Neil Young, Cohen, Tim Buckley y Joni Mitchell. Las mujeres recuperan su estatus de seres filosóficos: Phranc, Suzanne Vega, Tracy Chapman, Melissa Etheridge, Michelle Shocked, Barbara Manning, Lucinda y Victoria Williams, Indigo Girls y, en Canadá, Jane Siberry, Mary Margaret O'Hara y Sarah McLachlan. Excéntricos: Jandek, Daniel Johnston, David Thomas, Alejandro Escovedo; en California, Stan Ridgway, Chris Isaak y Smog. En Gran Bretaña, Billy Bragg, Robyn Hitchcock, Julian Cope y, la voz más importante de la década, Nick Cave, predicador del apocalipsis moral (From Her To Eternity, The Good Son). Sinéad O'Connor, Sting, Morrissey, Momus; el pop celta de Enya y Loreena McKennitt; al cambiar la década, Joe Henry, Daniel Lanois y Bob Mould.

mentions.text: …overlooked, delighted Canada: Blue Rodeo's keyboardist Bob Wiseman (1) penned the hilarious philosophizing of In Her Dream (1989), Renowned producer Daniel Lanois (1), born in Canada but relocated to New Orleans, reconstructed "roots-rock" from an "ambient" (impressionistic, atmospheric, rarefied) perspective…

podcast.title: Rise in 1993
podcast.body: Daniel Lanois began his rise in 1993, joining a wave of new Canadian artists gaining attention both domestically and internationally. This marked a period when foreign music fans started discovering Canadian talent. "1993, Doe Boys, the Tea Party, Daniel Landwaw, More Sarah McLaughlin, More Pursuit of Happiness, More Cowboy Junkeys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of the 90s CanRock Explosion

podcast.title: "Science Teacher" Role for "Where the Streets Have No Name"
podcast.body: During the recording of U2's "Where the Streets Have No Name," he used a large blackboard and a pointer, acting as a "science teacher," to visually guide the band members, particularly the rhythm section, through the complex time signature changes (from 6/8 to 4/4) in the song's intro. "I was in, I was the science teacher so I had the pointer and I pointed at the chord changes as they came around."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: U2 and The Joshua Tree at 30 with Daniel Lanois Part 1

podcast.title: Another Roadside Attraction Tourmate
podcast.body: Daniel Lanois was a Canadian performer who toured with The Tragically Hip's Another Roadside Attraction festival in 1993, 1995, and 1997. "Tourmates included Canadian performers like Daniel Landwass, Spirit of the West and the Rio Statics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Birth and Early Life
podcast.body: Daniel Lanois was born in Hull, Quebec, in 1951. Following his parents' divorce, he moved with his mother to Ancaster, now a suburb of Hamilton. "Daniel was born in Hull Quebec in 1951 when his parents divorced he moved with his mom to Ann Caster, which is now a suburb of Hamilton."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakthrough with U2
podcast.body: Lanois's big break came in 1984 when Brian Eno, recruited by U2 to evolve their sound, brought Lanois onto the project, leading to the creation of "The Unforgettable Fire" album. This album was a breakthrough for both U2 and Lanois. "Then came the Big Break. In 1984 Eno was contacted by U2 to help them take their sound to the next level and when Eno finally agreed to take the job he called up Dan and held it and the result was the unforgettable fire."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Canadian Heritage
podcast.body: Identifies as Canadian and humorously claims responsibility for originating the "toque thing." "Listen man, I’m Canadian, I started the toop thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: U2 and The Joshua Tree at 30 with Daniel Lanois Part 1

podcast.title: Collaborative Production with Brian Eno
podcast.body: Daniel Lanois co-produced U2's "The Joshua Tree" with his personal friend, Brian Eno. Their role was unconventional, involving not only classic production tasks but also playing instruments and singing backing vocals on certain tracks during the album's recording. "tanto, Brian Nino como Daniel Lanois, a trabajar durante el álbum no solo en trabajos de producción, sino que tocaron instrumentos durante la grabación del álbum, pero incluso a sus voces figuran en los coros algunas de las canciones."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Discovered by Brian Eno
podcast.body: Daniel Lanois, a young Canadian musician, was discovered and subsequently mentored by Brian Eno, who "took him under his wing." "along the way he discovered this young Canadian kid called Daniel Lannwan, took him under his wing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Recording Experiments in Hamilton
podcast.body: Prior to working with U2, he conducted experiments in an old, vacated Hamilton library building (constructed in the 1920s or 30s) which offered unique acoustics with its "endless corridors and labyrinths and beautiful foyers and mezzanines." The city provided him with keys to this building, allowing him to record rock and roll records in spaces that were more reverberant or dense than his own padded studio, seeking expansive recording environments. "I had already experimented in the old Hamilton library because the library had relocated and the building they vacated was a beautiful building. I think built in the 20s or 30s and it had endless corridors and labyrinths and beautiful foyes and mezzanines"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: U2 and The Joshua Tree at 30 with Daniel Lanois Part 1

podcast.title: Early Studio in Mum's Basement
podcast.body: With his brother Bob, Daniel Lanois established a studio in their mother's basement, where they assisted hundreds of local bands in recording demos. "Together with his brother Bob, they set up a studio in Mums Basements where they helped local bands record demos and apparently hundreds of groups made their way through that basement."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Global Residency
podcast.body: Daniel Lanois has been traveling extensively around the world and has no plans to return to Canada, citing better financial opportunities ("no U2 style money") and high taxes in his home country. "Daniel Lanai has been bouncing all over the world and has no intention of coming back."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grand Avenue Studios
podcast.body: In 1976, Lanois secured a job at the newly opened Grand Avenue Studios in downtown Hamilton, spending extensive hours producing records for various artists, including children's entertainer Rafi. "In 1976 Dan got a job at a new recording studio in the east end of downtown Hamilton called Grand Avenue Studios where he spent countless hours making records with tons of different performers including Rafi, the children's entertainer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Interviewed Artist
podcast.body: Daniel Lanois is among the notable artists and bands that have been interviewed. "Daniel Lannoy, some 41, Billy Corgan..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joshua Tree Studio Client
podcast.body: Daniel Lanois is mentioned as a client of the studio located in Joshua Tree, California. This facility, which serves as both a recording space and the owner's home, was also used by the Foo Fighters for recording their song "Outside." "and Daniel N.Wa."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kingsway Studios
podcast.body: In the mid-1980s, after he and his brother sold Grand Avenue Studios, Lanois considered opening a studio in Mexico before choosing a mansion in the French Quarter of New Orleans, which he named Kingsway Studios. "In the mid 1980s Daniel Landwom is brother-sold Grand Avenue Studios. Dan then started looking for a new headquarters and at first he thought about building a studio someplace in Mexico but in the end he sailed on a mansion in the French Quarter of New Orleans. He called it Kingsley Studios."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mentorship by Brian Eno
podcast.body: Brian Eno, impressed by a track Lanois produced for Time Twins, booked studio time with Lanois at Grand Avenue. Over several years, Lanois gained extensive knowledge about recording music while working on Eno's early ambient records. "Eno was so impressed that he booked time with Dan at Grand Avenue to work on some of his early ambient records and over the next couple of years Landwom learned a lot about recording music which he then applied to sessions with bands like Martha and the Muffins and the Parachute Club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Passion and Guitar Talent
podcast.body: From a young age, Daniel Lanois developed a deep passion for music, particularly the guitar, and was significantly influenced by Jimi Hendrix. In his mid-teens, he was recognized as one of Hamilton's top guitar players and also gained a reputation for being a valuable presence in a recording studio. "Daniel got deep into music, especially the guitar and especially Jimmy Hendrix by the way. In his middle teens Daniel was recognized as one of the best guitar players in all of Hamilton."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ownership of Infinite Sustain Guitar
podcast.body: Daniel Landwom possesses one of the three "infinite sustain guitars" invented and built by Michael Brook. "He built one for himself, for Edge and then I have the third one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: U2 and The Joshua Tree at 30 with Daniel Lanois Part 1

podcast.title: Producer for 12 Bar Blues
podcast.body: Daniel Lanois, a Canadian producer, was responsible for producing Scott Weiland's solo album, 12 Bar Blues, released in 1998. "producing it was Canadian Daniel Landwine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Production Partnership with Brian Eno
podcast.body: Collaborated with Brian Eno from late 1979 to early 1980s, producing "half a dozen ambient records in Hamilton" and developing a "textural sound" that they later brought to U2. "I had been working with Brian late 1979 to, let’s say, late 82, 83. We made a half a dozen ambient records in Hamilton and we had refined this textural sound that Brian was very excited about"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: U2 and The Joshua Tree at 30 with Daniel Lanois Part 1

podcast.title: Respect for the Rhythm Section
podcast.body: Larry Mullen of U2 specifically wanted to work with Daniel Landwom on "The Joshua Tree" due to Landwom's reputation for having a strong respect for the rhythm section. "Larry Melon once and he said one of the reasons he wanted to work with you on the Joshua Tree was because you had a real respect for the rhythm section."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Nash the Slash (Jeff Plunman, Toronto, 1948–2014) – Surgical Bandages Adopted After Three Mile Island Accident (1979); David Gilmour Offered Guitar Part but Nash Refused All Guitars
xref.body: Nash the Slash's real name was Jeff Plunman, born in Toronto on March 26, 1948. The stage name came from a character in a 1927 Laurel and Hardy silent film. He co-founded the prog band FM in 1975 and audiences could see his face briefly, but after the nuclear accident at Three Mile Island near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania in March 1979, Nash adopted surgical bandages that completely obscured his face as a way of raising awareness about what could happen if a nuclear plant melted down. He left FM around 1980 to resume his solo career, toured with Gary Numan and the Tubes, hung out with Iggy Pop and Daniel Lanois, and Brian Eno collaborated on his records. David Gilmour of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs — but Nash refused because he never used guitars on any of his songs. He made records until 2012, was especially popular in Germany and Poland, and died of an apparent heart attack at his Toronto home on May 10, 2014, at age 66. His music and costumes are managed by the Nash the Slash Legacy organization and much was donated to the National Music Center in Calgary. His best-known record was 1984's American Bandages. "David Gilmore of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs, but Nash refused because he never, ever used guitars on any of his songs."

xref.body: Malcolm Burn has had gigs producing and engineering for Bob Dylan, with Daniel Lanois's help. "With Dan's help Malcolm has had gigs producing an engineering for Iggy Pop and Patty Smith and Bob Dylan and Blue Road View and Midnight Oil and junk house and John Mellon Camp in many many more."

xref.title: Current Ownership
xref.body: Upon Daniel Lanois' departure to work with U2, Bob Doige assumed ownership and continues to operate the studio today. "When that happened, a guy named Bob Doige took over the studio and runs it to this day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Daniel Lanois Production
xref.body: Daniel Lanois, brother of former bassist Jostelyn Lanois, also contributed to the band's music by serving as a producer for some of their recordings. "Brother Daniel also produced music for Martha and the muffins."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Discovery of Daniel Lanois
xref.body: Brian Eno is responsible for discovering and mentoring Daniel Lanois, a young Canadian musician, taking him "under his wing" and helping to launch his career. "along the way he discovered this young Canadian kid called Daniel Lannwan, took him under his wing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Diverse Production and Engineering Work
xref.body: With the assistance of Daniel Lanois, Malcolm Burn has produced and engineered for a variety of artists including Iggy Pop, Patti Smith, Bob Dylan, Blue Road View, Midnight Oil, Junkhouse, and John Mellencamp. "With Dan's help Malcolm has had gigs producing an engineering for Iggy Pop and Patty Smith and Bob Dylan and Blue Road View and Midnight Oil and junk house and John Mellon Camp in many many more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Lineup and Collaborations
xref.body: Michelle McAdory and Greg Keelor were joined by Jostelyn Lanois, sister of producer Daniel Lanois, on bass, and Ambrose Pottie on drums. The band frequently opened shows for Blue Rodeo. "Michelle and Greg were joined on base by Jostelyn Lamwaw, sister of Super producer Daniel Landwaw. And on drums was the spectacularly named Ambrose Putty. Crash Vegas opened a lot of shows for Blue Rodeo back then."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: From Assistant to Producer
xref.body: Malcolm Burn was an assistant at Grand Avenue Studios and was later hired by Daniel Lanois to run Kingsway Studios in New Orleans. Like Bruce Fairbairn and Bob Rock, he transitioned from a band member (Boys Brigade) into full-time production. "And one of the guys he hired to run the place was an assistant at Grand Avenue named Malcolm Bern. Malcolm used to be in a band-2 they were called Boys Brigade but like Bruce Fairburn and Bob Rock Malcolm eventually got into producing full-time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Daniel Lanois
xref.body: Jimi Hendrix was a significant influence on Daniel Lanois, particularly in his passion for the guitar. "Daniel got deep into music, especially the guitar and especially Jimmy Hendrix by the way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Interest in Canadian Avant-garde
xref.body: Brian Eno, a British musical experimenter, showed interest in several avant-garde Canadian performers. This led him to a recording by "Time Twins" that Daniel Lanois had produced. "Brian Eno who at the time just happened to be interested in several avant-garde Canadian performers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: International Attention and Eno Collaboration
xref.body: The studio gained international recognition, hosting clients such as Rick James and Talking Heads. This attracted Brian Eno to Hamilton, where he met Daniel Lanois. Lanois and Eno collaborated on several small projects before Eno invited Lanois to work on U2's *The Unforgettable Fire* album. "And this is how Brian Eno came to work in Hamilton where he met Daniel Landwaw."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Kevin Spencer's Post-Rhymes with Orange Career
xref.body: Kevin Spencer, originally from Hamilton, joined Rhymes with Orange in 1996. He later performed in the touring version of the musical *Rent* for over 500 performances and also worked and toured with Daniel Lanois. Currently, he lives and works in music in Atlanta. "Kevin Spencer, who is originally from Hamilton, joined the band in 1996 and then went on to be a performer in the touring version of the musical Rent. He appeared at over 500 performances."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

"In 1984 Eno was contacted by U2 to help them take their sound to the next level and when Eno finally agreed to take the job he called up Dan and held it and the result was the unforgettable fire."
